findings.title: Denial cache key drops identity type and collides anonymous with renderer
findings.body: Check builds the denial-cache key from only the subject id (checkReq.UserUID), not the identity type. This package's own Check tests use subjects "anonymous:0" and "render:0", so both parse to UserUID "0" and share one key for the same namespace, action, name, and folder. The denial lookup at the start of Check returns Allowed:false on any hit, before getRendererPermissions or anonymous permission logic runs. Renderer is supposed to be allowed dashboards:read, folders:read, and datasources:read unconditionally, but an anonymous deny for that dashboard (or the reverse, a renderer deny for an action anonymous is allowed) sticks for shortCacheTTL (30s) and 403s the other identity. Image rendering, alert screenshots, and anonymous access can deny each other.

findings.title: Denial cache key joins name and parent with underscore, so distinct resources collide
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates name and parent with "_", but both values are resource UIDs and Grafana UIDs may contain underscores. A deny for dashboard "report" in folder "q1_2024" and a check for dashboard "report_q1" in folder "2024" produce the same key (namespace.perm_<user>_<action>_report_q1_2024). Check treats any hit as definitive deny and does not consult permissions, so one resource's deny is applied to the other for 30 seconds. That is a wrong authorization decision, not just a missed cache optimization.

findings.title: Sticky denial cache skips the DB refresh and outlives a stale folder tree
findings.body: A denial-cache hit in Check returns Allowed:false immediately and never reaches the new path that reloads permissions when the cached scope set does not allow the resource. Denials are also stored whenever the post-refresh checkPermission call is false, including when the negative answer came from the cached folder tree rather than from fresh permission rows. checkInheritedPermissions returns false if ParentFolder is missing from that tree, which is exactly the case for a dashboard just created in a new child folder whose access is inherited from an ancestor. Folder cache and denial cache are both 30s, but they are written at different times, and nothing deletes a denial when permissions are later reloaded or the folder tree is rebuilt. So a check that races permission insert, or that runs while the folder tree is stale, keeps 403ing for up to 30s even after a later reload has already cached the grant. That reintroduces the creator lockout this PR is fixing, and a refreshed perm cache cannot override the denial because the denial entry is consulted first.
